summary: This memo updates RFC 3168, which defines Explicit Congestion Notification. It relaxes restrictions that hindered experiments aiming at benefits beyond avoiding packet loss, and summarizes the areas where experimentation is expected.

plainLanguage.summary:
Explicit Congestion Notification lets routers tell a sender that the network is congested instead of throwing the packet away. RFC 3168 set down exactly how senders and routers must react, and those rules stopped researchers from trying anything else.

This memo keeps the old rules as the default but allows an Experimental RFC to change them. It covers three kinds of experiment: reacting less strongly to a congestion mark, treating the two ECN codepoints differently in the network, and using ECN on packets such as connection requests and retransmissions that were previously excluded.

subtitle: Loosening the rules on Explicit Congestion Notification so it can be experimented with.

tldr.problem: The base ECN specification ties senders and routers to fixed behaviour: a congestion mark must be treated exactly like a lost packet, the two ECN codepoints must be treated alike, and ECN must not be used on TCP control packets or retransmissions. Those rules block experiments that would get more out of ECN.
tldr.mechanism: The memo rewrites the affected sentences of the ECN specification so that the old behaviour is the default but may be changed by an Experimental RFC. The same treatment is applied to the ECN rules for RTP and for three DCCP congestion control profiles.
tldr.outcome: Three kinds of experiment become possible: a different sender reaction to a congestion mark, different marking for the two codepoints, and ECN on TCP control packets and retransmissions. It also retires the ECN nonce experiment and frees the ECT(1) codepoint for new work.

facts.label: IPv6 servers setting both ECT codepoints

today: RFC 8311 is a Proposed Standard from January 2018. It updates RFC 3168 and the ECN rules for RTP and DCCP, and it has not been obsoleted. The changes it makes are permissions rather than behaviour: the old rules still apply unless an Experimental RFC says otherwise.

sections.title: Why the ECN Rules Blocked Experiments
sections.content:
Explicit Congestion Notification, specified in RFC 3168, is an alternative to packet drops for telling endpoints that the network is congested. This memo relaxes restrictions in RFC 3168 that hinder experimentation towards benefits beyond just the removal of loss.

The restriction that mattered was procedural as much as technical. RFC 3168 is a Proposed Standard, and changing it normally needs the full standards process. The memo puts all of the enabling changes in one place so that an experiment can proceed without needing a process exception for each Experimental RFC that wants to change RFC 3168. Any experiment still has to be described in its own Experimental RFC, but as long as the change stays inside the bounds this memo sets, no exception is needed.

There is no need for this route when a mechanism is documented in a Standards Track RFC, since such an RFC can update RFC 3168 directly. The memo also makes related updates to the ECN specification for RTP in RFC 6679 and for three DCCP profiles, RFC 4341, RFC 4342 and RFC 5622, for the same reason. RFC 5622 is itself an Experimental RFC, and it is modified here only for consistency with the other two.

One of the anticipated experiments uses the ECT(1) codepoint that had been dedicated to the ECN nonce experiment in RFC 3540. The memo records the conclusion of that experiment and gives the reason for reclassifying RFC 3540 from Experimental to Historic, which frees the codepoint for new experimental use.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules for ECN were written as fixed requirements. Changing them meant going through the full standards process every time. This memo takes the three most limiting rules and turns them into defaults that an experiment may override.

sections.title: Three Areas of Experimentation
sections.content:
The memo covers three areas, and points to other documents for the detailed goals and rationale of each. It expresses no view on the likely outcome of the experiments and does not specify them in detail.

Congestion Response Differences. An ECN congestion indication tells the receiver that a short queue exists at the bottleneck with higher likelihood than a dropped packet does. That suggests a different sender response may be appropriate, such as backing off by a smaller amount than it would for a loss. This is at variance with the requirement in RFC 3168 that a sender's congestion response to ECN congestion indications be the same as to drops.

Congestion Marking Differences. Congestion marking at network nodes can be configured to keep very shallow queues, together with a different sender response to the marks, as proposed in the Low Latency Low Loss Scalable throughput work. The traffic involved has to be identified by the senders to the network nodes, to avoid harming other traffic whose senders do not expect the more frequent marking. Using the two codepoints differently, ECT(0) and ECT(1), is a promising way to identify that traffic, but it is at variance with the requirement in RFC 3168 that traffic marked ECT(0) not receive different treatment in the network than traffic marked ECT(1).

TCP control packets and retransmissions. RFC 3168 limits the use of ECN with TCP to data packets and excludes retransmissions. With ECN deployed in large parts of the Internet, there is interest in extending the benefits to TCP control packets such as SYNs and to retransmitted packets, as proposed by ECN++. This is at variance with RFC 3168's prohibition of ECN for those packets.

The scope of the memo is limited to these three areas. Additional experiments in them are possible, for example on using ECN to support a protocol similar to Data Center TCP beyond its current applicability in data centre environments. The stated purpose is to remove the constraints in Standards Track RFCs that stand in the way.
sections.plainLanguage: Three experiments are unblocked. A sender may react differently to a congestion mark than to a loss. Routers may mark the two ECN codepoints differently, so that one kind of traffic can get very short queues. And ECN may be used on connection requests and retransmissions, which used to be excluded.

sections.title: Network and Operational Considerations
sections.content:
ECN is becoming widely deployed and is being designed into further protocols. Experiments are expected to coexist with the deployed ECN functionality, and the responsibility for that coexistence falls mainly on the designers of the experimental changes. The memo gives three guidelines to avoid conflicts.

First, the forwarding behaviour described in RFC 3168 remains the preferred approach for routers that are not taking part in an ECN experiment, in particular continuing to treat ECT(0) and ECT(1) as equivalent. Second, a network node must not assume that the CE codepoint means the packet would have been dropped if ECN were not in use. Congestion Response Differences experiments use different congestion responses to dropped packets than to CE-marked packets, so CE-marked packets should not be arbitrarily dropped. A corresponding difference in congestion responses already happens when the ECN field carries Pre-Congestion Notification. Third, a network node must not originate traffic marked ECT(1) unless it is taking part in a Congestion Marking Differences experiment that uses ECT(1).

Some experiments use ECN on packets where it has not been used before, specifically TCP control packets and retransmissions, and the new middlebox behaviour requirements there are of particular importance. In general, any system or protocol that inspects or monitors network traffic should be prepared to encounter ECN usage on packets and traffic that currently do not use it.

ECN field handling requirements for tunnel encapsulation and decapsulation are specified in RFC 6040, which is itself being updated, and related guidance for encapsulations whose outer headers are not IP headers is given elsewhere. Those requirements apply to all traffic, including traffic that is part of any ECN experiment.

Changes in traffic behaviour are likely to affect network operations and management. Designers of ECN experiments are expected to anticipate the effects and consider how to deal with them. The topics to consider include possible network management changes or extensions, monitoring of the experimental deployment, collecting data for evaluation, and possible interactions with other protocols, particularly ones that encapsulate network traffic. The RFC points to RFC 5706 for more.
sections.plainLanguage: Networks that are not part of an experiment keep their current behaviour. A router must also stop assuming that a marked packet would have been dropped, because the whole point of the experiment is that the sender reacts differently to the two cases.

sections.title: The ECN Nonce and RFC 3540
sections.content:
RFC 3168 uses two ECN-Capable Transport codepoints, ECT(0) and ECT(1), to say that a packet supports ECN. The second codepoint, ECT(1), was assigned to support the ECN nonce functionality, which discourages receivers from exploiting ECN to improve their own throughput at the expense of other users. That functionality was fully specified in RFC 3540.

The nonce worked as specified and had been deployed in limited environments, but widespread use did not materialise. A study of the ECN behaviour of the top one million web servers, using 2014 data, found that after ECN was negotiated none of the 581,711 IPv4 servers tested were using both ECT codepoints, which would have been a sign of nonce use. Of the 17,028 IPv6 servers tested, four set both ECT(0) and ECT(1) on data packets. That might have been evidence of nonce use, but it might equally have come from a middlebox or router re-marking the ECN field incorrectly.

With new experimental functionality that depends on ECT(1) for other purposes, continuing to reserve the codepoint for the nonce is no longer justified, and other approaches to discouraging receivers from exploiting ECN have emerged. The memo therefore declares the ECN nonce experiment concluded, notes the absence of widespread deployment, and updates RFC 3168 to remove the discussion of the nonce and of the use of ECT(1) for it.

Four changes to RFC 3168 do that work: removing the paragraph in Section 5 that follows Figure 1, which gave the nonce as the motivation for two codepoints; removing Section 11.2 in its entirety; removing the last paragraph of Section 12, which said ECT(1) might be used as part of an ECN nonce implementation; and removing the first two paragraphs of Section 20.2, which discuss the nonce and alternatives. The rest of Section 20.2, which discusses alternative uses for the fourth ECN codepoint, is left alone.
sections.plainLanguage: The ECN nonce was an idea for stopping a receiver from cheating on congestion signalling. It worked, but nobody used it. Measurement of the top million web servers found almost no sign of it, so the codepoint it had reserved is now free for other experiments.

sections.title: The Updates to RFC 3168
sections.content:
Each update takes the same shape. The original sentence in RFC 3168 keeps its force, and a short clause is added saying that an Experimental RFC in the IETF document stream may say otherwise. Nothing changes until such a document appears.

For Congestion Response Differences, the change allows the congestion control response to a CE-marked packet to differ from the response to a dropped packet, provided the change is documented in an Experimental RFC. This is applied to the requirement that a sender's congestion control response to a single CE packet must be essentially the same as to a single dropped packet, and to the rule that on receiving an ECN-Echo acknowledgement the TCP source halves the congestion window and reduces the slow start threshold. No update to RFC 4774 is needed, because it quotes the text as background and imposes no requirement on it.

For Congestion Marking Differences, several changes are needed. Routers are allowed to treat ECT(0) and ECT(1) differently, again only if an Experimental RFC says so. The rule that a router should set the CE codepoint only if it would otherwise have dropped the packet is changed so that congestion indications which are not equivalent to drops are allowed. A larger update replaces the two paragraphs that let senders use either codepoint freely and explain why two codepoints exist: in their place, protocols and senders must use ECT(0) unless an Experimental RFC says otherwise, and must not use ECT(1) unless an Experimental RFC says otherwise.

The memo also states that a Congestion Marking Differences experiment should modify the network behaviour for traffic marked ECT(1) rather than ECT(0) if only one codepoint's behaviour is changed, and must not modify the behaviour for ECT(0) traffic in a way that requires changes to the sender congestion response. If an experiment does change ECT(1) behaviour in a way that needs a matching sender change, the Experimental RFC must state both the sender congestion response to CE marking and the router behaviour changes, or the absence of them.

For TCP control packets and retransmissions, the change allows ECT codepoints on SYN and SYN-ACK packets, pure acknowledgement packets, window probe packets, and retransmissions of packets that were originally sent with an ECT codepoint, again provided an Experimental RFC says so. This removes the prohibition in RFC 3168's Section 5.2, that an ECT codepoint must not be set in a packet unless the loss of that packet would be detected by the end nodes and interpreted as congestion, and the prohibitions in Sections 6.1.1, 6.1.4, 6.1.5 and 6.1.6.

RFC 3168 is silent on whether a network element such as a firewall may discard such a packet as invalid. The memo adds text saying that middleboxes should not discard TCP control packets and retransmitted TCP packets solely because the ECN field does not contain Not-ECT. There is an exception for responding to an attack that uses codepoints other than Not-ECT, for example dropping ECT-marked TCP SYN packets with higher probability than SYN packets marked Not-ECT, but such discarding must not be done routinely in the absence of an attack and should only be done if the use of ECN is contributing to it.
sections.plainLanguage: Every change works the same way: the old rule stays, and a note says an experiment may override it. Nothing changes in practice until someone publishes such an experiment.

sections.title: The Same Changes for RTP and DCCP
sections.content:
The ECN rules for RTP in RFC 6679 get the same treatment. That document lets a sender use either codepoint and says it should mark packets ECT(0) unless the receiver asks for ECT(1) or for a random ECT value using the ect parameter in the a=ecn-capable-rtp: attribute. Because the Congestion Marking Differences work raises the consequences of using ECT(1), two sentences are added: random ECT values must not be used, since that may expose RTP to differences in network treatment between the two codepoints and to the associated endpoint congestion responses, and ECT(0) must be used unless an Experimental RFC says otherwise.

The RTP response to a CE-marked packet is also relaxed. RFC 6679 said the reception of CE-marked packets must produce a congestion notification that makes the algorithm react as if packet loss had occurred, and that there should be no difference in congestion response between CE marks and packet drops. Those two sentences become conditional on an Experimental RFC saying otherwise, and a following sentence that allowed other reactions to be specified in future is changed to allow a Standards Track RFC or an Experimental RFC.

The three DCCP congestion control specifications, for congestion control IDs 2, 3 and 4, all contain the same wording: each DCCP-Data and DCCP-DataAck packet is sent as ECN Capable with either the ECT(0) or the ECT(1) codepoint set. The memo replaces that with wording that keeps the ECN Capable requirement but says that such senders must set ECT(0) unless an Experimental RFC says otherwise. All three RFCs also lose their discussion of the ECN nonce.
sections.plainLanguage: The same rule is applied to the other two protocols that use ECN. RTP and DCCP senders may use the second codepoint only when an experiment says so, and for now they should use the first.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
As a process memo that only relaxes restrictions on experimentation, the document has no protocol security considerations of its own. The security considerations of any experiment that takes advantage of the relaxed restrictions belong in the documents that propose those experiments.

The memo does place one responsibility on experimenters. Effective congestion control is crucial to the continued operation of the Internet, so the responsibility for not breaking Internet congestion control falls on the experiments and on the people proposing them. That responsibility includes the requirement that an Experimental RFC discusses the congestion control implications of the experiment, and review of that discussion by the IETF community and the IESG before publication is intended to give assurance that each experiment does not break Internet congestion control.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo adds no security rules of its own. It does insist that each experiment explains how it will not break congestion control for everyone else, and that the review process checks that explanation.

viz.caption: The four values of the ECN field in the IP header

items.label: Not-ECT
items.desc: Set by senders whose transport does not support ECN.

items.label: ECN-Capable Transport 0
items.desc: Set by a sender whose transport supports ECN. Senders must use it unless an Experimental RFC says otherwise.

items.label: ECN-Capable Transport 1
items.desc: The second capable codepoint. Senders must not use it unless an Experimental RFC says otherwise.

items.label: Congestion Experienced
items.desc: Set by an intermediate node to say that congestion was seen.

viz.caption: The three experiments this memo unblocks

items.title: Congestion response differences
items.text: A sender may react less strongly to a congestion mark than to a lost packet, because a mark suggests a short queue rather than an overflow.

items.title: Congestion marking differences
items.text: Routers may mark traffic marked ECT(1) more often than traffic marked ECT(0), which lets them keep very short queues.

items.title: TCP control packets and retransmissions
items.text: ECN may be used on SYN and SYN-ACK packets, pure acknowledgements, window probes and retransmissions.

viz.caption: The rules that keep experiments from harming the rest of the network

items.title: Routers keep treating both marks the same
items.text: Forwarding behaviour from RFC 3168 stays the preferred approach for routers not taking part in an experiment.

items.title: A mark is not a drop
items.text: A router must not assume that a CE-marked packet would have been dropped, because CE-marked packets should not be dropped arbitrarily.

items.title: Do not originate ECT(1)
items.text: A network node must not originate traffic marked ECT(1) unless it is taking part in a marking experiment.

items.title: Expect ECN in new places
items.text: Systems that inspect traffic should be prepared to meet ECN on packets that do not use it today.
